![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14187261/assets/97a7d465f8412c88367ed3cf148af3ce387441284c10e3f84888c0186fa597ce.png)

Peter wants to cut a piece of square-shaped glass while maintaining its shape. The area of this glass is decreasing at a rate of $1.5{\text{ in}}^{2}/\text{min}.$ At what rate are the diagonals of the glass decreasing if the length of these diagonals is $50\text{ in}?$
question.worked_solution:
Let $h$ and $A$ be the length of the diagonals and the area of the square, respectively. Using the Pythagorean theorem, it can be shown that the relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{h}\cdot \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $A$ decreases at a rate of $1.5{\text{ in}}^{2}/\text{min},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we want to compute the rate of change of the diagonals when the diagonal has length $h=50.$ Substituting this information into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{50}\cdot (-1.5) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1.5}{50} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-0.03\,\text{in}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the diagonals of the glass are decreasing at a rate of $0.03\text{ in}\text{/min}.$
